HEADLINE: Where are they now?
TEXT:
The Young Rich List turns 15 this year and its debutants have grownup.Their fortunes have grown too,mostly.

When the first Young Rich List was published by BRW in September 2003, John Howard was immovable from The Lodge, Pauline Hansonwas in jail and the launch of Facebook was five months in the future.

But one thing hasn’t changed: Australia was, and still is, a great place to make money. The economy grew3.6 per cent in 2003-04, about the same clip that the Reserve Bank expects the economy will grow in 2018-19 as it enters its 28th year free of recession.

The average Australian could have picked up the 2003magazine and recognised many of the Young Rich Listers’ names from the worlds of sports (Harry Kewell, Luc Longley, Pat Rafter,Grant Kenny, Lleyton Hewitt, KarrieWebb), acting (Nicole Kidman, Russell Crowe, Cate Blanchett, Guy Pearce) modelling (ElleMacpherson) and music (DarrenHayes and Daniel Jones from Savage Garden, Kylie Minogue).

These days, the property and technology booms have long since swept the entertainers aside. Few actors and sports stars are able to keep up with the fortunes made by developers – be they in the business of developing software, apps or high-rise apartments. Two notable exceptions are Miranda Kerr, now married to Snapchat billionaire Evan Spiegel, and soccer star Kewell, whowas just 24 when that first list appeared. Now aged 40, he’s made the Young Rich team for one last season before he reaches the cut-off age of 41. Kewell is the list’s only perennial.

Two of the under-40s that appeared on the first Young Rich List enjoyed a seamless transition to its parent, and remain on what is now known as the Financial Review Rich List.

Michael Boydwas ranked second on 2003’sYoung Rich List with a fortune estimated at $160million. The Perth accountant had made his fortune by buying into a struggling pathology and diagnostics company in 1992,when he was aged 27, and turning it around. Boyd left Sonic Healthcare’s board as 2003’s list was being published, but Medicare and cashed-up Baby Boomers mean his family’s 3.6 per cent stake was still the main reason he placed 169th on the 2018 Financial Review Rich List, with a $511 million valuation.

Greg Goodman was one of the 2003 Young Rich Listers who was helped by a wealthy background – his father Sir Patrick Goodman co-founded the Goodman Fielder food manufacturing empire. However, the wealth of $66 million ascribed to him at the time recognised his efforts in building up the family’s industrial property vehicle, Goodman Group. It made a pre-tax profit above $1 billion for the second time in 2017-18, putting Goodman, 55, comfortably on this year’s Rich List in 70th place.

Another member of the class of 2003 is MYOB co-founder Craig Winkler. In 2009 he took his $125million cheque from the sale of the desktop accounting software and put $15million of it into Xero, MYOB’s cloud-based disrupter. That stake is now worth $715million, but you’ll no longer find Winkler on the Rich List. An active Christian, it emerged this year that the deeply private entrepreneur is donating nearly all the money to charity, via the appropriately named Givia trust.

Meanwhile, the richest young Australian of 2003 also rose to the 2018 Rich List, in spirit. John Ilhan, of “Crazy John’s” mobile phone stores fame, died suddenly of a heart attack in 2007. His business partner and widow, Patricia, sold the chain to Vodafone in 2009, reportedly for $150million. She ranked 194th on the 2018Rich Listwith a $407 million fortune, no longer invested in Nokias but in property and managed funds.

The opposite of the Rich List is where 2003’s fourth-richest Australian under 40, Eddie Groves, found himself after the collapse of his ABC Learning Centres childcare business in 2008. Bankrupted with debts of $23million in 2013, he of the mullet and snakeskin cowboy boots was permitted by a court to move to Canada, where it was reported he and wife Viryan Collins-Rubie have set up a language school. Groves’ bankruptcy ended in 2016.

Another 2003 Young Rich Lister to find notoriety after the global financial crisis, Gordon Fell, has kept an even lower profile.

On the eve of the GFC, Fell sold his debt-laden real estate business Rubicon Group to the greater fools invested in Allco Finance Group, escaping with the money to buy Sydney’s then-most expensive house, “Routala” at Point Piper.

Coincidentally, that harbour side home is back on the market with a $55million price tag, nearly double what Fell paid in 2007.

He and wife Phillipa appear to have moved back into the professional property speculation game, in April registering a business called Sequitur Hotels.

Falling the most is former Billabong boss Matthew Perrin who, along with wife Nicole, was number seven on the inaugural Young Rich List. In January he was sentenced to eight years’ jail for fraud and forgery after a jury found him guilty of writing his wife’s signature on loan documents as he tried to bail himself out of bad bets on Chinese shopping centres during the GFC.

But most of the class of 2003 have not experienced such Rich List-sized rises or vertiginous falls. They have just been plugging away.

The editorial in that 2003 issue of BRW proclaimed, “the entrepreneur is back”.

Stories like Perrin’s aside, many more of its inaugural Young Rich Listers have helped stop “entrepreneur” becoming the dirty word itwas after the dotcom crash, and the Christopher Skase and Alan Bond scandals before that.

One of the entrepreneurial heroes on that original list is Janine Allis. In 2003 her $14 million fortune was derived from her Boost Juice retail chain, back then amounting to 11 company-owned stores and 62 franchises.

Today her empire, known as Retail Zoo, stretches to 500 stores in 14 countries across four brands: Boost Juice, Salsa’s FreshMex, Cibo Espresso and Betty’s Burgers. “There are as many stores overseas as there are in Australia,” Allis tells The Australian Financial Review Magazine about the globalisation of her business over the past 15 years.

Allis and husband Jeff sold 70 per cent of Retail Zoo to The Riverside Company for nearly $70 million in 2010, before another private equity giant, Bain Capital, swooped in 2014. Allis still has a minority stake in the business. These days she’s a star of Network Ten’s Shark Tank and is also on the board of ASX-listed jewellery retailer Michael Hill.

“I’m having a ball really. I’m getting older but I’m having fun,” Allis says. The same could be said for Brett Godfrey, the former Virgin Blue high-flier who these days prefers to walk. Godfrey’s Tasmanian Walking Company has just opened its fourth trail on the island, a 46-kilometre jaunt through the Tasman National Park with a couple of eco-friendly luxury lodges along the way.

Godfrey turned 40 a month before the 2003Young Rich List was published, and a couple of months later took Virgin Blue public in a deal that added considerably to the $12million fortune that had placed him 50th. “I can assure you that it didn’t dome any favours at home,” he recalls of the publicity from appearing on the list.

Not only did Godfrey have to sell Australians on no-frills flying, he had to do it fighting tooth and nail against one of the great airline executives in Qantas boss Geoff Dixon. Ironically, Dixon is now his business partner in developing walking tracks on the mainland through the Australian Walking Company.

You won’t hear Godfrey complain that 2018’s crop of Young Rich have it any easier than he did. “I think they have it ‘different’ these days, not better and not worse,” he says. “Pre-2000, entrepreneurs were building businesses that usually made ‘stuff’ or traded ‘stuff’.

“Today’s billionaires have largely come from good or great technology ideas, that thanks to social media and the internet are offered the opportunity to go viral. That didn’t exist 20 years ago, and the near perfect knowledge prospect it presents can be a huge advantage vis-à-vis earlier entrepreneurs.”

But while technology entrepreneurs have become a Rich List force, Godfrey still believes there are plenty of opportunities outside it. Indeed his Tasmanian Walking Company is pitched at getting people into nature and away from their phones, away from social media and the distractions of the web. “Environmental tourism is where I leverage my investments and businesses these days,” he says. That’s a business model that could have worked 15 years ago, and almost certainly will be just as much in vogue in 15 years from now.

Perth’s Mark Barnaba, who hit the list with an estimated $18million wealth in 2003 after selling a corporate advisory business, went on to become Macquarie Group’s West Australian chairman. He now sits on the Reserve Bank board and is co-deputy chairman of Andrew Forrest’s Fortescue Metals Group. Barnaba says building your own business and “doing your own thing and in your own way” is much better understood and valued today than it was 15 years ago.

While financing has become easier – there are more options and better-developed early-stage capital markets – the pace of change means today’s entrepreneur needs to move faster. “There is less time today to perfect one’s business model and adjusting quickly to change and to technological innovations isn’t just important, it is essential for survival,” he says.

That said, the ingredients for success haven’t changed thatmuch. “You need a good idea, the ability to spot the opportunity others don’t, and extremely hard work.” ●

With Fiona Carruthers and Julie-anne Sprague.

HEADLINE: Other Passions
TEXT:
ALEXANDER LOTERSZTAIN | Founder of Derlot design studio | Age: 41 | Lives:CampHill, Brisbane

mountain biker?

My first bikewas a BMX, and I remember at age five or six I cut my head open attempting a jump.Whenmy parents gaveme a mountain bike I was hooked. I was doing two things I liked – riding and exploring.

I'moriginally fromArgentina, andwhen I was 16 a friend and I rode through Patagonia in our summer holidays. It took us about threemonths; we did about 2000 kilometres and camped in some absolutely magical places. That little moment in time, it reallymattered. Mountain biking is a really goodway of exploring the world at a different speed.

What's your preferred style of trail?

I don't like ones that are manicured, with the wooden boards and jumps and all that – I prefer touring. I like getting into very technical descents. It's even better when you find themby accident.

Yourecentlyrode thoughKazbegi NationalPark, on the border ofGeorgia andRussia.Whatmade you go there?

I often ride with my friends Florian Groehn, a Berlin-based photographer, andAaron Nielsen, a creative director working in Stuttgart.We'd done a lot ofmountain biking trips in the usual places, like crossing the Alps fromGermany toAustria, but it wasn't adventurous enough – we wanted to push the limits. Florian had visitedGeorgia two years before, and had all these images on file.Wewent, "Yeah, let's go there!" Whatwas the hairiest thing that happened on that trip?

We were on a walking trail, heading towards a glacier on the bottomofMountKazbek, which is one of the highestmountains in Georgia, and there was one section that was a sheer cliff.

At that point, we said, "If we're going to do this, we're going to have to go really slow." Itwas a tight turn with the bike. If I had misjudged it, I would have been dead for sure. I managed to stay on the bike, but Florianwalked it because it was just too risky.

Youhave twoyoungdaughters(agedsix andfour).Does thatmakeyoumore cautious on the bike?

A little bit. Butwhat I get out of it on a self-growth level far outweighs the risk.The thing about mountain biking touring is that everything is a new trail. It never gets easy.

You just have to embrace that. And it becomes addictive; you actually seek not knowing the trail.

We all have our daily routines, but it's so difficult to switch off – when you get home and turn onNetflix,work is still always there.When I'mmountain bikingmy focus is 100 per cent on the task ahead, becausemy life depends on it.

Hasmountainbikingaffectedyour approach to yourwork as a designer?

Not really. I thinkwhat it's givenme is a kind of attitude, the idea that you can overcome any challenge that comes your way.

So, you'veneverhada"eureka"moment on the bike ?

No.When I'mdesigning,which is something I'mvery passionate about, it's a 24-hour thing. I go to sleep, I dreamon it, andwhen I wake up I sketch on it.

Mountain biking erases those thoughts.

I'm concentrating on something completely different. It's refreshing, like a mental break fromthe rest of your life. ●

HEADLINE: The Chosen Ones
TEXT:
It’s what’s on the outside that lure wine buyers to the beauty inside.

What differencedoesawelldesigned wine label make? In the case of Canberra District producer Four Winds, the answer is a 50 per cent increase in sales.

In late 2015, FourWinds commissioned Sydney-based wine-packaging design specialists Denomination to revamp its labels. Launched in 2002 by chief executive Rowena Curlewis and creative director Margaret Nolan, Denomination’s client list ranges from corporate giants such as Penfolds to small family wineries such as FourWinds. It has 25 staff and offices in London and San Francisco.

“Australians tend to be naturally open and outward looking,” Curlewis says. “I think this has an impact on how we design.

We’re not constrained by traditions, as they tend to be in Europe, or genres, as they tend to be in the United States. Our design has a variety and a freshness of thinking that I think comes from being Australian.”

In 2017, Denomination won four trophies and was named agency of the year at the Harpers Design Awards in London, and at the 2018 Drinks InternationalWine Design Awards it was named supreme champion for the second consecutive year.

“We try to solve two problems for clients,” says Nolan. “First, the label has to stand out on the shelf and appeal to consumers. Second, we try to tell the client’s brand story really powerfully. In the case of FourWinds, they had professional labels but it didn’t say anything about them as people or as a business. When we looked at their Instagram account, though, it was full of evocative imagery of life on the vineyard.We latched on to that and integrated it into the labels, to create something that was emotive and credible.”

This ability to design appropriately for each client – type-heavy labels for Yalumba’s The Caley; bold, ultra-modern labels for Yabby Lake Vineyard – is what led Four Winds to Denomination.

In the 18 months following the re-launch of the FourWinds labels – and with no other changes to the marketing or promotion of the business – sales rose almost 50 per cent and gross profit lifted 135 per cent; the cellar door was welcoming two-and-a-half times more visitors and wholesale distribution more than tripled. Importantly, employee numbers grew from three to 14.

The FourWinds labels helped Denomination sweep the floor at Harpers and at Drinks International, but the gongs that mean most to Curlewis and Nolan are the Design Effectiveness Awards, announced annually by the London-based Design Business Association. This year, they picked up a goldmedal for the FourWinds redesign.

“These awards are the holy grail in the design industry,” says Curlewis. “It is super, super hard to get a medal there. All sorts of things are entered – train timetables, plane seats – and the designs are judged not just on how good they look, but also on the impact they’ve had on the client’s business.”

“That’s the ultimate accolade for me,” says Nolan. “When our packaging can help a brand become really successful.”

Rowena Curlewis, left, andMargaretNolan of Denomination Design, in their Sydney office.

Yalumba The Caley, 2013 Barossa / Coonawarra $350 The classic design of this bottle suits both the name on the label – it’s an homage to a colourful ancestor of the family that owns Yalumba – and the classicallyproportioned, elegantly-structured “claret” inside.

Yabby Lake Single Vineyard Pinot Noir, 2017 Mornington Peninsula $64 Designed back in 2002 but still fresh and distinctive, the Yabby Lake Vineyard label is a modern classic. And the wine in the bottle is superb: a preally vibrant, juicy, deeply complex and rewarding young pinot noir.

FourWinds Sangiovese, 2016 Canberra District $30 Each of the labels in the FourWinds range picks up on the breezy theme. This one, featuring a disintegrating dandelion, is particularly evocative and whimsical, and thewine – cherry-fruited and savoury – is delicious. ●

HEADLINE: All fired up
TEXT:
Chef JulianHills gets hands-onwithmore than the food atNavi, his deliberately small (25 seats) and dramatically dark dining roomtucked behind a heritage shopfront in the inner-westMelbourne suburb ofYarraville.

“I oftenseeadish inmy mind, long before I start building in the flavours,” says Hills. The Victorian chef and potter started cooking part-time in the late 1990s to fund his fine arts degree, but by the time he passedwith honours, he wanted to be a chef.

The past six years have been spent running the kitchen at the one-hatted Paringa Estate at Main Ridge,where Hills forged close relationships with theMornington Peninsula’s small-scale growers.

They supply every ingredient in Spring at Main Ridge, (pictured right), which is dish number two on Navi’s eight-course degustation menu ($120). “I love seeingwhat I can dowith the whole plant,” says Hills. The dinner might start with black garlicmacaron with salmon roe, and finish with strawberry gum sorbet with pickled quandong.

Hills finds strong parallels between cooking and ceramics.

“Both require a lot of recipe work, testing, and control of temperatures.” He makes all his plates, too. “They’re not perfect in any way,” he says. “That’s why I like them.”

The sea-green table top is froma large hunk of sun-damaged marble found in a stonemason’s backyard which Hills mounted on an old table.Other tables at Navi are made from recycled mountain ash; raw and industrial; or from a local furniture-maker.

Ducasse afloat in Paris

On the first fully electric cruise boat in Paris, you will hear little more than the clink of glassware as you drift down the Seine dining on turbot in champagne sauce prepared by Alain Ducasse, the most Michelin-starred chef in the world. Launched in September after an investment of about €11 million ($18,000), the 300-tonne Ducasse Sur Seine was designed by naval architect Gerard Ronzitti, with a sparkling glass interior from Maurizio Galante and Tal Lancman. In another first for Parisian river-boat cruises, the 36-strong kitchen team preps everything from scratch on board. Lunch and dinner cruises cost from €100 to €500, or enjoy an aperitif while the vessel is moored.

Anchoring the dish is a rich, light feta cream, made with goats’ milk from the 200 individually named “girls” of Main Ridge Dairy. “Their milk is so beautiful in spring, it’s inspiring,” says Hills.

Hills works on the “if it grows together, it goes together” maxim, tucking in black nasturtium leaves, edamame, broad beans, peas, pea tendrils, broad bean flowers and lemon balm in such a natural way that they look as if they have grown on the plate.

The rich and vibrant green-pea ice-cream can only bemade for a few weeks of the year. “In spring, there is just enough sugar in the peas for it to work as a dessert,” says Hills.

The warm “soil” is a crumble of peas and almonds. Pureed peas are spread on a sheet and dehydrated, then blitzed into powder, mixed with almond meal and gently toasted.

Trend alert! The soft, dusky notes of a black garlic – garlic that is fermented for weeks until it softens and turns black – add earthiness to the base.

Ducasse afloat inParis Around theworld on a table

How does a table designed by a Dane and named for Madrid turn out to be so well-suited to an Australian lifestyle? The new Madrid six-seater table designed by Morten Georgsen for BoConcept (from $2439) has a timeless, simple beauty, from its powder-coated concrete base to the silk-painted white glass top that seems to float above. It also commemorates the 25th year Georgsen – who defines his work as “elegance with purpose” – has been designing cool, space-saving tables for Denmark’s leading global furniture group. Feel free to cover it with everything from Scandi smørrebrød to Spanish tapas.We’re in Australia, after all. ●

HEADLINE: Fragility Within
TEXT:
Reading Matters

Name your favourite childhood book.

Childhood was long; I can’t name just one.

At five it was Clifford the Big Red Dog by Norman Bridwell, about a dog trying to fit into suburbia. I liked the premise and the pictures. At 12 it was the Photography Year Book 1972, a compendium of awardwinning images, from politics to street gangs and art nudes in nature.

Which books have inspired yourwork?

My grandfather was an Air Force chaplain in Korea and he brought back a 15thcentury Buddhist text which is woodblock printed on soft, now stained, parchment.

My great-uncle left us An Alphabet, an illustrated book byWilliam Nicholson published in 1898. It is screen-printed with spot colours, and the colours are still rich on the page, thicker and more vibrant than anything printed today.

Thebestbookyouhaveeverread? In Cold Blood by Truman Capote makes you empathise with the human condition and question our morality and how we govern ourselves. It feels like a work of fiction, when we know that it isn’t.

Whathaveyoureadrecentlyforwork and enjoyed? From the Earth by Peter Gilmore, a cookbook and botanical book in which Peter and his wife Kath write passionately about long-forgotten and newly rediscovered vegies. The photography by Brett Stevens is on another level.

Bohemian Living is a coffee-table book in which photographer and author Robyn Lea goes into artists’ homes and documents their worlds. She touches on themes of childhood and family and how the artists surround themselves with objects, light and colour to make an environment that feeds back into their work.

Are thereanybooksyouwishyouhad designed? Not really. I do, however, have a “that’s bloody genius” moment of awe and appreciation when I see some covers. Book designers likeW. H. Chong and Josh Durham deliver regularly on that front.

What are you reading now?

The Happiest Refugee by Anh Do. I was interested in Anh’s art and his story. It’s a ripper – a poignant, fast-paced page-turner with heart and humour.

Shell Kristina Olsson Scribner Brisbane writer Kristina Olsson’s exquisite new novel is steeped in art, politics and family. Set in Sydney in 1965, against the background of the building of the Opera House and the Vietnam War, it is also a love story between Pearl, a feisty Australian journalist, and Axel, a Swedish glassmaker. It is Olsson’s fifth book; her most recent, Boy, Lost: A Family Memoir, won several literary awards.

After Pearl’s mother dies when she is 14, Pearl and her younger brothers, Jamie and Will, are sent to a convent. Pearl escapes to become a journalist, and as the novel opens, she has not seen the boys for six years. She is desperate to find them because conscription has been introduced and they are of an age to be sent to Vietnam. Axel, haunted by his own demons, has come to Australia to work with architect Jørn Utzon to design the foyer to the Opera House.

Shell is a book about loss, grief, and guilt.

Pearl’s life is shaped by the gaping wound left by her mother’s death and by the guilt she feels for abandoning Will and Jamie. Axel feels guilty about his father’s disappearance when he was young, something he had sometimes wished for. When they meet, their connection is immediate.

Shell is also about politics. The Vietnam War is a constant presence, and Olsson never lets us forget its impact on individual lives. Pearl has been demoted to the women’s pages of her newspaper after being photographed attending a protest march. Later, her phone is bugged.

The escalating battle between Utzon and his political masters is portrayed as a struggle between art and petty politics, idealism and pragmatism.

Axel wonders if the politicians fear that the sheer beauty of Utzon’s design might make people want more “kindness, tolerance, more beauty”. Shell is a celebration of artistic endeavour, as Axel, too, strives for perfection. A classic in the making.

The Land Before Avocado Richard Glover ABC Books What was Australia really like from 1965 to 1975? Were we really better off then than we are now? In his latest book, The Land Before Avocado, bestselling Sydney author and journalist Richard Glover challenges nostalgia for days past by reminding us of things we would rather forget. The result is a very funny recap of the decade, laced with some sobering reminders that it was not all safari suits and fondue.

Glover has trawled through old newspapers and magazines to present a broad overview of Australian society back then, covering everything from schools, food and fashion through to racism, endemic sexism and censorship. There are priceless nuggets of information – in the interests of frugality women were advised to use cut beetroot as rouge – as well as alarming facts about the White Australia Policy, fault-based divorce and the fact that until 1983 a married woman needed her husband’s permission to leave the country. The Australia of that period was not, he notes, a great place to be if you were a woman, gay, a migrant or Indigenous.

The Land Before Avocado will have you laughing out loud in recognition if you lived through this era, and incredulity if you did not.

Normal People, set in Ireland a few years ago, is about the relationship between Connell and Marianne, who meet in high school. Marianne’s family is wealthy – Connell’s mother is their cleaner – but troubled. At school she is a misfit; when she and Connell start seeing each other, they keep it a secret. The situation is reversed when they start college – Marianne is now confident and popular, whilst Connell is neither. Soon they are dating again, seriously, and so marks the beginning of a rollercoaster ride as their relationship lurches from intimacy to miscommunication.

Rooney’s description of Marianne’s and Connell’s thoughts and feelings is authentic and nuanced, and their conversations are brilliant. It is also an insightful illustration of how close two people can be, and how they can influence each other’s lives, for better or worse. ●

HEADLINE: Hold the time
TEXT:
Smart watches want to make themselves indispensible to an ageing population.

Aconfession. I stoppedwearing the Apple watch. Since its release in Australia three years ago, I had worn it every day on one wrist while rotating favoured mechanical timers on the other.

I have loved the Apple’s design, the straps you could swap out at will, its legibility, and found various functions useful – if mostly about what my body was up to rather than the time of day.

And that’s partly the problem – get over being obsessed about the speed your heart is pumping at, or how many steps you’re taking, and the Apple watch might as well be just another device, one with no hint of the earthy charisma so comfortingly offered by mechanical timepieces, let alone the chore of charging.

The fall-off in appeal shouldn’t have come as a surprise given that for timepiece tragics like me the best watch is always the next one. That means something new or the latest iteration of something already on our wrist.

(How many Rolex Submariners or Speedmasters is that you have now, dear?) In other words, Apple might merely be proving to be beholden to the same rules as any other brand, namely the demand for constant updating to keep it appealing.

Which brings us to the new version launched in September; is it different enough towin back lapsed wrists like mine and entice new devotees? And who is the target market for this clever device?

Is it the cool kids – of any age – who’ve always favoured Apple’s sleek offerings over those from HP, Dell, Samsung and the rest?

The brightly hued straps that can be swapped out would suggest yes. But anecdotal evidence, namely who I see wearing the Apple watch, suggests a somewhat older fan base.

Certainly it’s towards them that Apple’s clever boffins and app developers have looked in turning this year’sWatch Series 4 into a health essential more than an aid. For example, in addition to monitoring heart beats, it will have an app – due out in the United States later this year – that can record an electrocardiogram and detect irregular heart rhythms. A cardiologist who recently tried to kill me with a stress test told me that an Australian company, Alivetec, has already developed a watch strap and app combination that does this. He said you can send the result to your doctor, too.

The second headline concerning the new Apple watch takes us further into walking frame territory. Behold the fall detection feature, which measures g-forces, wrist trajectory and impact acceleration, before initiating a call to emergency services. Clearly not for the skateboard brigade.

Whether all this makes the Apple more a watcher than a watch is a fair question.

That said, there’s a stunning new display to look at, fresh Hermès versions to covet, new bands to mix and match. And if you want more than the time at your fingertips, it ticks a brilliant array of boxes. Let’s see if I fall for it.

Bani McSpedden is watch editor of The Australian Financial Review.

HEADLINE: Hot to trot
TEXT:
Today,wearegoing toexamineideal attire forwhen in close proximity to the muscular flanks of pounding thoroughbreds. Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to race wear.

It should be said that I am hardly an aficionado of the track. I did once judge Fashion on the Field, but that was up in Broome,Western Australia, where first prize went to the last person to wilt. I have been to Ascot with people posh enough to whisper that you pronounce it “Askit”. And of course, I have watched the race that stops our nation from under the brim of a hat; not at Flemington, but at a Melbourne Cup lunch in a Sydney restaurant where the floor was even, so no one had to worry about stilettos on grass.

That said, my advice on race wear is that you may as well dress as you bet – to win.

1. The hat. As I’ve talked about hats recently, just to add, a big brim also acts as a sunshade and you can’t say that of a fascinator. 2. Shoes. No one wants to be reminded of what happens to a lame horse. 3. Handbag. Why not copy the QueenMum? Choose one structured enough to work as a battering ram through the crowds to place your bets and capacious enough to store your winnings. Racing is all about hope, after all.

For what to wear in-between, I have sought expert advice from Stewart Parvin, who has a beautiful store on Motcomb Street in London’s Belgravia. He is a dressmaker of the highest order, which is to say he doesn’t impose, he listens to his clients’ needs. One of those clients is the most famous woman in the world of racing. Yet despite the “By Royal Appointment” gilded crest next to the store’s front door, our terms are clear. Not a word about the Queen.

What Parvin will talk about is the weather. “It will be unpredictable, whether you are headed to Flemington or Aintree,” Parvin pronounces. “The answer lies in layers you can take off and put back on. A light printed dress, with a light, long line coat is always appropriate.” Shape? “Keep your outfit as understated as your accessories are not,” he says. Print? “The enduring popularity of print is explained because a race day is a long day. Print doesn’t show the creases like a block colour.”

Not that Parvin is anti bold colour (ref. the lime green, silk tweed ensemble HerMaj wore to the wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle). “Bold colours are far more flattering against a flushed face than pastels and nudes. Colour is the friend of the mid-life lady, the mature lady,” he says with infinite charm. Just as the structured jacket is better than floaty chiffon damp with perspiration.

His eternal tip for race goers of all ages? “The beach-towel tango. Change when you get there.” Pardon? Is it possible that Parvin, who looks like a gent at the races as imagined by Cecil Beaton in My Fair Lady, so immaculate is he in top hat and tails, changes in the Ascot car park?” “Of course! I drive there in shorts.” Does, then, his most famous client perhaps do her own version of a last-minute change in the royal coach? “Good try,” he laughs and leaves it there. ● International fashion editor Marion Hume is based in London.

HEADLINE: Forecast
TEXT:
Hermès has taken the plunge into surfing with its Savana Dance board. Crafted by Ardmore, a South African collective made up of Zulu, Zimbabwean and Sotho artists, its pigmented resin hull is shaped for stability and agility, the top of the board and the two fins reinforced with maple veneer. And if looks aren’t enough, infused into the surfboard is a scent developed by Hermès Perfumes creative director Christine Nagel. $10,995 (02) 9287 3200

Berluti’s Off the Road range of eight accessories includes biker boots, a bum bag, briefcase, gloves, wallet and backpack. But it’s this ultralight helmet combining a carbon-fibre shell and edges underlined with patinated Venetian leather, as well as a handmade leather visor and eyeshade, that revs our engine. $6250. berluti.com

Italian architect Renzo Piano has collaborated with the Royal Academy of Arts in London for the Art of Making Buildings, a 30-year retrospective of his career. The exhibition follows Piano’s design legacy and includes rarely seen drawings, models, photographs and full-scale maquettes, along with a specially designed sculptural installation which brings together nearly 100 of Piano’s projects. Until 20 January. royalacademy.org.uk

Based in Venice, California, No.One creates handmade bespoke and limited-edition sneakers and desert boots.

The lamb-skin lining is from northern France and the tanned leather tongue is sourced in Tuscany. The shoes, such as this Bravo in Speckled Pony Hair, come with a lifetime guarantee. $US675. no-one.la

Loewe creative director Jonathan Anderson presented his Spring Summer 2019 at Paris fashion week in a space re-invented as a contemporary art gallery. The show featured installations by artists including Loewe Craft Prize finalist, basketweaver Joe Hogan.

Anderson set ostrich feathers against topstitched gabardine; Peter Pan collars in exotic leathers; ruched tops had bishop, bell and Juliet sleeves. Bags were in woven calfskin and thatched in straw; baskets featured floral raffia.

loewe.com

HEADLINE: Osmosis
TEXT:
Little did you know that the hotel foyer you enter is actually an experience in brand immersion.Nor that the restaurant you dine at is more sensory journey than mere trip for the tastebuds. And it’s Fabio Ongarato’s job to ensure that you never need to.

In 1979 NASA realised that a space station it had abandoned five years earlier was starting to break apart and it hadnoway of predictingwhere itwould crashtoearth.

As the world’s media speculated on what might happen, in the early hours of July 12 Skylab disintegrated overWestern Australia’s south coast, scattering scrap across theNullarbor Plain and putting Perth, for a fewhot minutes, on the edge of one of the biggest stories on the planet.

Visitors to the city’s new QT hotel, which opened in August, wouldn’t know it but when they check in they’re standing on a memorial, of sorts, to Skylab’s fall. In the lobby, 3D computer renderings of silver surfaces collapse into a kind of shinymagma glimmer like somuch disco debris on the walls. The disintegration of the US space station may seem unusual inspiration for a hotel billing itself as “an eclectic mix of style and luxury” but Fabio Ongarato is nothing if not a lateral thinker.

“We loved the idea of metallic objects falling to earth,” says Ongarato. “Wewanted to tell a story thatmirrored the city itself, from elemental mining town to hotbed of ’80s excess and future glam.”

Neither architect nor interior designer, the Melbourne-based creative is a brand whisperer, an art director turned teller of narratives intended to elevate consumer experience. He’s the guy behind the elaborate branding of Crown Metropol, the mastermind of Aesop’s digital archive (known as the “Taxonomy of Design” and viewable online) and it’s his signage and assorted visual cues that help workers and clients navigate ANZ’s headquarters in Melbourne’s Docklands. His fingerprints are throughout Jackalope, the hottest of hotels, on the Mornington Peninsula.

The Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney and the National Gallery ofVictoria have both called upon Ongarato’s services and now he’s working with the ArtGallery of NSWwhile also providing a brand refresh for the Art Gallery of South Australia. At this year’s Spring Racing Carnival, punters lucky enough to be invited into the newVictorianRacingClub stand at Flemingtonwill get a taste of Ongarato’s work on all five levels.

His influence is almost everywhere, even if at times it seems toseep into thewoodwork. Inthe caseofQT Perth, once you’ve moved past the glinting metallic finishes in the foyer, you might notice native flora, such as kangaroo paw, liquefied into giant abstractions, its fibrous hairs taking on an alien allure. At ground level, mineral tones and psychedelic flora dominate, the mood becoming ever more ethereal the higher guests venture. It’s a futuristic phantasmagoria doubling as a hip hospitality option.

ToOngarato’smind it’s all a narrative, but one that tries to sidestep cliché. “It’s about moving beyond the kind of iconography that you would typically see on a picture postcard,” he says.

The same game is being played across the entire QT portfolio of hotels. For QTMelbourne, near the “Paris” end of Collins Street, Ongarato borrowed notions of burlesque, French noir films and crime thrillers; for Sydney, in the old Gowings and State Theatre building, it’s all about exhibitionism with shop dummies cavorting in provocative poses; Canberra has head shots of legendary leaders, from Che Guevara andMargaret Thatcher to Barack Obama and Bill Clinton. The figure of Tony Abbott greets guests in the elevator.

“He’s a purist who’s not afraid to push boundaries,” says Marita Burke, creative director of Mecca Cosmetica, with whomOngaratoworks to develop brand identity, packaging design, in-store graphics and the like. “He even works with our architects tobring the brandtolife, really crystallising the brand identity in whatever form it manifests. Fabio takes the world of design toamuchmore intellectual level. I always feel like we’re getting a global standard, locally.”

Indeed that is the level on which Ongarato often plays.

Fabio Ongarato Design, which he co-founded with Ronnen Goren, has 38 staff in its Melbourne office and operates branches in Hong Kong and Dubai, with clients such as W Hotels. Having just turned 25, it has instigated its own jubilee refresh, renaming itself StudioOngarato and resetting its compass to navigate the choppy waters of the experience economy.

A turning point came in 2010, when then-ANZ Banking Group chief Mike Smith sought help to devise more of a “breakout culture” in the bank’s Melbourne headquarters thatwouldencouragestaff toleavetheirdesksandcollaborate.

“The interior architects atHassell had devised a floorplan with all these breakout areas scattered about andweworked with them around core themes of move, play, grow and create,” says Ongarato. “It was about workplace happiness, quite a big benchmark in 2010.”

“What was remarkable about the ANZproject,” saysRobertBackhouse, chairman of international design practiceHassell, “was that Fab and the gang were involved right from the concept stage andwithinamonth they were embedded in an integrated and collaborativewaywithour team.They look at things from such a strong conceptual, multidisciplinary perspective, which allows them to constantly come up with really cool stuff. They are quite likely to say something like, ‘Hey, we should do a crazy neon light thing over there!’ and make it happen.”

Ongarato’s crazy neon light thing at ANZCentre is a zippy, white, ceiling-mounted sculpture which hovers above a “Move” hub, a fire-engine red breakout zone abutting an espresso bar.

Having worked with Ongarato for the past 25 years, Backhouse says the pair have developed a shorthand to spur one another on. “‘I’m not sure that’s very good’ means ‘it’s crap’ and ‘is that the best thing you’ve ever done?’ means ‘it’s really crap’.Happily,we don’t have cause to say either often   Fabio Ongarato was born in the north Melbourne suburb of Oak Park in 1971, the son of Italian immigrants.

Educated with theChristian Brotherswhich he found “pretty frightening”, his parents detected early artistic leanings and engaged an Italian painting teacher to offset what he remembers as the rough and tumble of school.

“I always loved the Italian Renaissance, of course, the perfection of the composition of a bowl of fruit and the dramatic lighting of a meticulous landscape.”

He studied visual communication at RMIT, where his cultural referencesexpandedtoembrace thefilmic extravagance of Bernardo Bertolucci and his storied cinematographer Vittorio Storaro, often referred to as a painter of light for such masterpieces as Last Tango in Paris and The Last Emperor.

Other influences included German photographer Helmut Newton“whoalwayshad threepointsof tension inhis images, for instance a huge stiletto, crazy hair and a leg brace on a beautiful, gargantuanwoman”; the fashion ofMartinMargiela which elevated the anonymous and the everyday through deft manipulation to the realm of the extraordinary; and the fragrance advertising of Viennese designer Helmut Lang who engaged conceptual artist JennyHolzer towrite the famous “I SMELL YOU ON MY SKIN” refrain which was variously printed and projected around theworld.

He graduatedwithhonours in1992asAustraliawas inthe midst of then-prime minister Paul Keating’s “recession we had to have” and set up his design studio the following year.

“In a way, the recession was a godsend for me because, fresh out of school, I was necessarily agile, with no structure and no baggage.The giants of the time likeGary Emery andKen Cato had toweather the economic storm, while for me it just made things seem really exciting.” Goren, who was studying in the architecture department at RMIT about the time Ongarato was hunkering down in vis-comm, was another early client. He was putting together an exhibition of postwar Jewish architecture in Melbourne and needed someone to develop the graphic collateral. The pair hit it off, discovered they shared a passion for culture and communication, and decided to team up under the banner of Fabio Ongarato Design. Today, Goren is responsible for strategy and new business, while Ongarato concentrates on creative direction – although both admit to a lot of cross-over in the roles.

“More byosmosis thananything else,we discoveredwe had a business,” says Ongarato. “We weren’t so much concerned with the traditional idea of a design studio and howwe should relate to that. At the time in Australia there was a lot of opportunity forus togrow, topush the existingparadigms and mould our own ideas ofwhat a design studio could be.”

As human-centred strategies become the catch-cry of the architecture, design and urban-planning professions, Ongarato is increasingly using narrative design – a paradigm which arose a decade ago in video-game development – to create “total immersions” that extend a brand’s offer beyond product to encompass experience. (In geek speak it’s referred to as “narratology” and has been retroactively applied to storytelling as far back as Aristotle.) Naysayers dismiss the decorative obfuscation of narrative design, its drive to add unnecessary layers to corporate brands and fluff up bereft architectural structures with empty “meaning”. If a brand or a product or an interior had real integrity, the argument goes, why would they need additional padding?

Ongarato insists that a contemporary art practice might offer a whole new perspective to a corporate brand. The beauty of collaborating with designers, artists, writers, illustrators and architects, he says, is that it opens up a dialogue on design.

In 2007 he was one of 50 graphic designers from around the world invited by the LondonDesignMuseumto create a graphic work to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Swiss typefaceHelvetica, paragon of modernist precision and font of choice for corporations as varied as American Airlines, Evian,Nestlé, American Apparel and Comme deGarçons.

Ongarato devised an oversizedHelvetica treatment of the nonsensical word “supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from the 1964 Disney musical, Mary Poppins. “I loved the idea of doing something quite stupid with something so incredibly precise,” he laughs.

For the W hotel Shanghai, which opened in February, the Ongarato team took core brand values, defined as “bold, wittywith a lust for life”, anddevelopedthese intoanarrative around “captivating contrasts”. These are expressed through vibrant visual cues, froma kaleidoscopic brass mirror mural behindthe receptiondesk, designed to reflect themultitude of cultures and influences (and hotel guests) flowing through the city, to a neon installation punctuating the lobby with lighting crafted to incarnate Shanghai’s “lilong” tradition of hanging wet laundry from lines stretched across narrow laneways. In its visual cacophony it effectively encapsulates the chaotic exuberance of the city.

“One brand, one experience is no longer enough,” says Goren, citing a 2013 JWT Intelligence Study which found that 78 per cent of Millennials wanted brands, products or entertainment producers tomake an active attempt to capture their imagination, while 61 per cent ofMillennials put a high priority on the “wow” factor. Whatever that might be.

At Melbourne’s Kisumé restaurant, Ongarato and team elaborated a slightly askew – to not say kinky – view of Japanese traditions by focusing spotlights on bondagethemed black and white photographs by controversial Japanese artist Nobuyoshi Araki. Playing on the tension between aesthetic refinement and sexual subversion, Araki’s work is renowned for the frisson that arises when beauty rubs up close to danger. In a similar manner, the designer’s use of circular graphics in other interior elements subtly inverts the Japanese flag – turning tradition on its head.

“While consumers are nowmore attuned, and resistant, to overt advertising, they are hungry for authentic experiences that shift theirperspectivesoroffer themsomethinggenuinely enriching,” says Ongarato. “Embedding a sense of culture into a brand can be extremely alluring.” ●
